title: a year of service designed
hook: better your own work done imperfectly than someone else's done well

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first piece of a year of service designed: sarvabhutahite ratah, delighting in the good of all beings. Whose good did you write down? Day nine hundred seventy.
screen: `A YEAR OF SERVICE DESIGNED.` · `THE GOOD OF ALL BEINGS.`

segments.voice: Somebody online is rebuilding houses after a flood. Somebody else is running a soup kitchen, fostering dogs, teaching kids to read. It's inspiring, and it can also leave a person frozen, scrolling through other people's good work and wondering whether their own is too small to count. The Gita has a verse for that exact paralysis. Krishna says it in chapter three, and then, as if he wants to be sure Arjuna heard, says nearly the same thing again near the end of the book. Today's piece of the design is where: which service is actually yours.
screen: `OTHER PEOPLE'S GOOD WORK.` → `FROZEN, SCROLLING.` → `WHICH SERVICE IS YOURS?`

segments.voice: We heard this line in passing a few days ago. Today it gets a closer look. Here's the verse, in paraphrase. Better your own dharma, even done imperfectly, than the dharma of another done well. The word is svadharma. Sva means one's own. Dharma is a big word, duty, right order, the way a thing is meant to work, and here it's the duty that belongs to your actual place in life. In the Gita's setting, Arjuna is a warrior, and Krishna is telling him not to trade his own hard task for someone else's that looks easier or holier. In chapter eighteen the line comes back, with an added note: by doing the work that belongs to your own nature, you don't incur fault. There it comes right after verses on the duties of the four varnas, the classes of the old social order, each said to arise from its own nature. Hindu readers have argued about how to apply that. Older readings tie svadharma to varna, caste, and stage of life. Some modern Hindu teachers read it more as the duty that fits your nature, your gifts, your situation, and that reading has its critics as well. And notice the word imperfectly. Krishna isn't promising your service will be impressive. He's saying it will be yours. For designing a year of service, that changes the first question. Not what's the most admirable work out there, but what's mine to do. The parent of a small child may have a year of service that looks like patience at bedtime and one shift a month somewhere else. A nurse might serve by not cutting corners on a tired night. Someone with a car might be the person who drives. The flood houses are real and good. They just might belong to someone else.
screen: `BETTER YOUR OWN, DONE IMPERFECTLY.` · `SVADHARMA: THE DUTY THAT IS YOURS.` · `READERS HAVE ARGUED OVER HOW TO APPLY IT.` · `NOT ADMIRABLE: MINE TO DO.` · then, large: `WHAT IS MINE TO DO?`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and breathe. Let three things come up, one at a time, without judging them. First, something you're simply good at, even if it seems ordinary: listening, fixing, cooking, explaining. Second, a place you're already in: a building, a group, a family, a route you drive. Third, a person who already relies on you. Breathe with each. Where do the three overlap? That overlap may be the start of your own dharma of service, imperfect and yours. If you pray, you can ask the one you pray to for clarity about it. The bell holds the time.
A year of service designed. Today's piece is svadharma: the service that belongs to your own life, better done imperfectly than another's done well.

segments.voice: Your line: a year of service designed. Today, write one sentence that starts, the service that's mine is, and leave it unfinished if it's not clear yet. Day nine hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers read the Gita's svadharma verses in more than one way, some tying them to caste and stage of life and others to a person's nature and situation; some people turn to the verse when weighing what kind of work or service is theirs.

fork.setup: you're Arjuna. another kind of life looks easier, maybe even holier, than the hard task that's yours. what does Krishna advise?
options: take the other path; it's done better there.
stay with your own dharma, even done imperfectly.
wait until you can do both perfectly.
fork.reveal: Krishna says your own dharma, even imperfect, is better than another's done well, and repeats it in chapter eighteen.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: svadharma, one's own dharma, from Gita 3.35 and 18.47.

trapdoor: what you thought: real service means doing whatever looks most impressive.
what it means: the Gita says your own dharma, done imperfectly, is better than someone else's done well.
what a scholar hears: svadharma in 3.35 and 18.47, read by older commentators through caste and stage of life, and by some modern readers through a person's nature.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.35 (better one's own dharma, though imperfect, than another's well performed)
